examples.knowledge_point: Solving Inequalities Requiring Division by a Positive Factor
examples.worked_solution:
First, we factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{x}^{3}+3x & <0. \\ 3x(2{x}^{2}+1) & <0\end{aligned}
$$

Since $2x^2 + 1$ is always positive, we can divide both sides of the inequality by this quantity. By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3x(2{x}^{2}+1)}{2{x}^{2}+1} & <\frac{0}{2{x}^{2}+1} \\ 3x & <0 \\ x & <0.\end{aligned}
$$

We know that the denominator ${y}^{2}+2$ is positive for all values of $y.$ So, we can multiply both sides of the inequality by ${y}^{2}+2$ and solve the resulting inequality as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4{y}^{3}+11y-5}{{y}^{2}+2} & \le 4y \\ ({y}^{2}+2)\cdot \frac{4{y}^{3}+11y-5}{{y}^{2}+2} & \le ({y}^{2}+2)\cdot 4y \\ 4{y}^{3}+11y-5 & \le 4{y}^{3}+8y \\ 11y-5 & \le 8y \\ 3y-5 & \le 0 \\ y & \le \,\frac{5}{3}\end{aligned}
$$
